narrative: The assessment estimated a 35% probability that you would become a bad credit risk. That does not mean default is certain—it implies a 65% estimated chance of good repayment—but it was above the bank’s risk limit for this application, so the loan was denied. The strongest influence was your checking-account status: a balance in the 0–200 DM range was the most important factor and pushed the decision toward bad credit. This is meaningful because approved applicants most often have no checking account (59.2%), while only 18.4% fall in this 0–200 DM range. The second most influential factor was your credit history, which worked in your favor and pushed toward good credit, even though it is recorded as critical/other credits. The third was the requested amount: 3,617 DM versus an approved-applicant average of about 3,020 DM; in your case this also leaned toward good credit, so it was not the reason for denial. Overall, the checking-account signal was the strongest and adverse enough that the favorable credit-history and amount signals did not offset it. Next, ask the lender which checking-account behaviors matter most, work on keeping a clearly positive balance and avoiding overdraft patterns, and request a review or correction of your credit-history record. Reapplying after improving the account status and clarifying your credit file would give you a stronger case.
